units.citation: Power et al. (2001). Deciduous or evergreen: Does it make a difference to understorey pasture yield and riparian zone management?. Proceedings of the New Zealand Grassland Association.
units.quote:
Shading of streams to lower water temperatures
and restore indigenous invertebrate and fish populations
is also an important consideration in any catchment
management programme that seeks to be sustainable
(Rutherford et al. 1999). At shading intensities of
70%, the amount of shade considered to benefit fresh
water fauna (Rutherford et al. 1999), pasture relative
yields could be reduced to approximately 53% of the
open pasture (based on Figure 1), without the added
influence of other tree effects reducing yields even
further.

relationship.outcome_raw: annual understorey pasture relative yield relative to open pasture, at the shade level needed to cool streams for fresh water fauna, read from the artificial-shade response curve

context.practice_as_described: Riparian zone plantings of trees to shade streams to the 70% shading intensity considered to benefit fresh water fauna; effect inferred from an artificial shade-cloth trial (0-83% shade, 4/8/12-month durations) on irrigated sown pasture. BASELINE: open pasture (100% relative yield).
context.note: Trade-off unit for the T6 production_gap target: a stream-shading riparian planting dense enough to meet the 70% shade target (Rutherford et al. 1999, cited) would cut understorey pasture yield to about 53% of open pasture, i.e. roughly a 47% loss (the 47 is our arithmetic, not encoded). Value read by the authors from Figure 1 (shade-cloth response curve), not measured under riparian trees; authors add other tree effects (litter smothering, moisture/nutrient competition) would reduce yields further, so this is a lower bound on the loss. Trial unreplicated (Bayesian smoothing, 83% CIs); soil moisture non-limiting (irrigated). Applies to pasture INSIDE the shaded riparian strip, not to the wider farm. Strength left unspecified: no BANDS row for a percent-of-control unit; |RR-1| = 0.47 would band as strong on the response-ratio rule. Not emitted: species comparisons under Acacia melanoxylon / Eucalyptus nitens / poplars (p3, Fig. 3; silvopastoral, not riparian, species-specific and figure-only values).

context.note: Round-7 decision t3t6r7_rb_heat (A): single narrative claim from a UK review, expected to give a weak riparian heat row. Country is the SRC default (UK review) - the cited studies' locations are not stated in the quote. hazard_type heat_stress: the quote names 'temperature stress' and livestock entering streams 'to cool down' (heat), though 'adverse weather (rain, wind)' also covers cold shelter. No heat event described (cf. Pete 2026-10-23 on ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3: general shade without a heat event is not T3 hazard mitigation) - round-7 A asks for the row anyway; orchestrator to confirm the hazard tag. Coded as microclimate_buffering (precedent: livestock shade units dobhal24/moran18), not livestock_productivity, so the one claim gives one unit (#61). Conclusion p8 restates it (justification quote). Same paragraph p5 also notes trees can compete with pasture/crop for light, reducing production (not emitted here).

All that is evident is that the majority of farms lost a great deal of canopy cover, an average of 37.5% canopy loss. 
The overall canopy loss was from an average canopy cover of about 40% before the hurricane to about 25% after 
the hurricane. This result is somewhat surprising given the expectation that shade cover, especially in the form of

context.practice_as_described: Biodrainage agroforestry model: four parallel strip plantations of clonal Eucalyptus tereticornis (Mysore gum, clone C-7) planted in December 2002 on raised ridges (0.5 m high) built along the field bunds of canal-irrigated, waterlogged farmers' fields at Puthi, Hisar, Haryana (northwest India). Strips were 66 m apart, each with two tree rows at 1 m x 1 m (300 plants per ha; 240 surviving); the strips occupied about 4% of the area and wheat was grown in the remaining 96% between them (p2). The deep-rooted, high-water-use trees act as 'bio-pumps' that transpire groundwater and lower the water table. BASELINE (comparator): adjacent canal-irrigated waterlogged fields without plantation (control observation wells 1 and 11; four untreated wheat fields).
context.note: Figure 4 'Trend of groundwater table levels in (a) transect I and (b) transect II at Puthi research plot during April 2005 and 2008' (p4). Wells 1 and 11 in the adjacent unplanted fields are the control (p3). Waterlogging here is chronic sub-surface waterlogging from canal seepage (groundwater within 3 m all year, surface waterlogging in the monsoon, p2), not an event year. Mechanism: tree transpiration of 268 mm per year against 212 mm mean annual rainfall, i.e. discharge 1.3 times recharge by rainfall (p6, Table 4); roots reached the capillary fringe at 2.80 m below the field surface (p4). Supersedes the second-hand reading in ev_waterlogging_hazard_singhlal18_1 (which gives 85 cm; the primary gives 0.85 m).

units.citation: Griscom et al. (2017). Natural climate solutions. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
units.quote:
Reforestation is the largest natural
pathway and deserves more attention to identify low-cost miti-
gation opportunities. Reforestation may involve trade-offs with
alternative land uses, can incur high costs of establishment, and
is more expensive than Avoided Forest Conversion (38). How-
ever, this conclusion from available marginal abatement cost
curves ignores opportunities to reduce costs, such as involving
the private sector in reforestation activities by establishing
plantations for an initial commercial harvest to facilitate natural
and assisted forest regeneration (39). The high uncertainty of
maximum reforestation mitigation potential with safeguards
(95% CI 2.7–17.9 PgCO2e y−1) is due to the large range in
existing constrained estimates of potential reforestation extent
(345–1,779 Mha) (14, 16, 40–42).
